newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Unique Swedish stamp sells for record $2.26 mln. [CORRECTED 16:37 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Unique Swedish stamp sells for record $2.26 mln. [CORRECTED 16:37 GMT]

text.p: A flimsy yellow 19th century Swedish postage stamp was sold by auction to a secret collector on Friday for 2.875 million Swiss francs ($2.26 million), making it the single most valuable postage stamp in the world.
The price to be paid, which includes 15 per cent commission, was an all-time record for one stamp, the Geneva-based Irish auctioneer David Feldman said.

Bidding for the stamp, the fabled "Treskilling Yellow", began at 900,000 Swiss francs ($705,000), and the price quickly ratchetted up over two million francs ($1.6 million) (Corrects dollar conversion from "$160 million" to "$1.6 million"), finally reaching 2.5 million francs.
Feldman declined to identify the new owner, but told Reuters: "I know who bought it. I had met this gentleman before, but I didn't know he was going to buy it."
The stamp, issued in 1857, was last sold at auction in 1990 -- also by Feldman in Zurich -- to a Swedish collector for 1.9 million francs.
"Over two million is incredible," said the auctioneer, who handles some of the world's top philatelic items. The price "will give people a lot of confidence who have bought rare stamps," he added.
The stamp, actually a dull orangey hue, has been hailed for almost a decade as the most valuable object of any type in the world proportionate to its weight, volume and density.

"I am very proud to have the honour to purchase the most valuable item in the world," said Hans Lernestal, the Stockholm dealer who bought the stamp for a private client. He said he would have been prepared to pay even more for it.

The stamp is so unusual it was once suspected of being a fake. But experts now generally believe it to be a unique misprinted version of a Swedish green three-shilling stamp issued together with a sheet of yellow eight shillings.
The Swedish post office has issued a commemorative version of the stamp, which has been feted at international exhibitions the world over.
Some of the world's top collectors, including the late King Carol of Romania, have owned it at various times since it first went on the market in 1885.

Bogdan Stanculescu, a Romanian collector at the auction specialising in early stamps from his country, told Reuters buyers generally fell into two classes: genuine collectors interested in the history of stamps, and investors.
"You can invest in something that has a big value. Or, there is another interest -- to have a special stamp," he said.
He estimated the number of collectors with the means to buy the "Treskilling Yellow" at only a handful, adding that it was possible that the person who bought it wanted to keep it in Sweden.
The stamp came up for sale after its latest owner, Sven-Olof Karlsson of Sweden, decided to sell rather than make final payments on the purchase he made six years ago.

Its 1.9-million-franc price even then made it the world's most valuable stamp, surpassing the legendary Mauritius Blue, sold in 1993 for 1.725 million francs ($1.35 million), also by Feldman's auction house.

The Treskilling Yellow was discovered by Swedish schoolboy Georg Backman in 1885. Visiting his grandmother at Christmas, Backman, 14, asked her to open a chest of drawers so that he could search for letters, hoping to find some old stamps to sell.
He took the yellow stamp and some others to a dealer in Stockholm who agreed to buy it for seven crowns, a modest sum.
Backman later recalled his visit to the dealer. "The expert was heard to mumble repeatedly: "But it is yellow.'"
"Finally I dared to ask him whether I was to receive seven crowns for the stamp, whereupon (he) answered: "I shall pay that much all the same.'"
A short time later Backman discovered that the dealer had already been offered 300 crowns for the rarity, but had declined to part with it, saying: "It will someday reach a very high price."
($1 = 1.2750 Swiss francs)
